Labile metabolic soft spots — unhindered aromatic rings, benzylic positions, N-dealkylation sites — lead to rapid first-pass metabolism. DILI arises through several mechanisms. Intrinsic (dose-dependent) hepatotoxicity occurs when a drug or its metabolite is directly cytotoxic to hepatocytes — acetaminophen (via NAPQI, its reactive quinone imine metabolite formed by CYP2E1) is the classic example. Idiosyncratic DILI is dose-independent and unpredictable, often involving immune-mediated mechanisms: reactive metabolites form covalent adducts with liver proteins, which can trigger adaptive immune responses (hapten hypothesis) or disrupt immune tolerance. Mitochondrial toxicity — inhibition of electron transport chain complexes or mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma — is another important mechanism. Bile salt export pump (BSEP/ABCB11) inhibition causes cholestatic liver injury by preventing bile acid secretion.

High lipophilicity (logP > 3) with extensive hepatic metabolism increases liver exposure to reactive intermediates. High daily dose (>100 mg/day) is a strong epidemiological risk factor.
